Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Anticoagulation and Foot Pain
Description: Discussion of anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation after prior gastrointestinal bleeding, with heel pain and diabetes follow-up.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports approximately one month of heel pain, especially on first arising in the morning, and ongoing knee discomfort. He has atrial fibrillation and has not been taking warfarin because of a prior gastrointestinal bleeding episode related to an ulcer. The clinician reviewed the benefits of anticoagulation for stroke prevention and the risks of recurrent bleeding. He reports good recent diabetes and blood pressure control but weight gain and increased appetite. His wife is receiving treatment for lung cancer. Nocturia persists while taking tamsulosin, although he drinks substantial fluids near bedtime. He also reports intermittent foot discomfort associated with footwear and positioning.
PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, previous gastrointestinal ulcer/bleeding, anemia, lower extremity pain, and urinary symptoms.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Heart rhythm was regular during this examination. Peripheral foot discomfort was discussed and examined.
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Atrial fibrillation with prior gastrointestinal bleeding: Plan careful reinitiation of Coumadin with anticoagulation clinic monitoring. Supply stool cards to check for recurrent occult blood after treatment is restarted. Reviewed warning signs and risks.
2. Heel and foot pain: Refer to Podiatry to evaluate footwear and possible custom inserts. Trial positional support at night.
3. Diabetes and weight gain: Continue therapy; counsel on portion control and activity as tolerated. Repeat laboratory testing before follow-up.
4. Nocturia: Continue tamsulosin at tolerated daily dosing; reduce late evening fluids.
5. Hypertension and previous anemia: Current control and improving blood counts reviewed; follow with laboratory testing.
Medications were renewed; return in approximately three months.
